title: Ratko Mladić: The monstrous crimes of the 'Butcher of Bosnia'
description: Image source, Corbis/Getty ImagesBySam WoodhouseRatko Mladić, who has died at the age of 84, was the bull-necked "Butcher of Bosnia".As Commander of t
body: Image source, Corbis/Getty ImagesBySam WoodhouseRatko Mladić, who has died at the age of 84, was the bull-necked "Butcher of Bosnia".As Commander of the Bosnian Serb army, he oversaw a brutal campaign of "ethnic cleansing" as Yugoslavia splintered in the 1990s.The phrase was a chilling euphemism for the massacre of tens of thousands of men, women and children - in pursuit of what he saw as a chance to fulfil the historic destiny of Greater Serbia. It was a goal he pursued with single-minded determination and studied brutality - and it made him responsible for the bloodiest atrocities Europe has witnessed since Hitler's Third Reich.His fanaticism made him a hero to his people. He told them their Muslim neighbours planned to "impale Serbs, burn them alive, crucify them and put out their eyes".He led the long and bloody siege of Sarajevo; killing and maiming its citizens in a daily hail of shells and sniper-fire. When his troops overran the UN-declared safe area of Srebrenica, he promised they were safe. Later, 8,000 men and boys were led to unmarked graves.He and his political counterpart, Radovan Karadžić, ripped Bosnia apart - committing acts of genocide and vicious crimes against humanity.The barrel-chested warlord displayed no remorse, giving relatives of his victims a cheery thumbs-up at his eventual trial in the Hague."Borders are drawn in blood," he is reported to have said. "And states marked out with graves."Image source, Sygma via Getty ImagesImage caption, A gravedigger buries civilians killed in the siege of Sarajevo in 1993Ratko Mladić was born on 12 March 1942 in a small mountain village near Sarajevo, then part of the German-controlled Independent State of Croatia - although he always claimed to be a year younger.Two years later, his father was killed fighting for Tito's partisans against Nazi-backed Croat nationalists. Mladić was brought up in the new, post-war construct of Yugoslavia. After a short apprenticeship as a tinsmith, he chose a military career.He graduated from officer school in 1965. Proving himself an ambitious and capable soldier, he rose rapidly through the ranks, commanding army units in Macedonia and Kosovo.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, General Mladić's troops laid siege to the Bosnian capital, Sarajevo, for 1,425 days. Thousands were killed by rocket and sniper fireTito's death in 1980 was the beginning of the end for Yugoslavia - always an uneasy confederation of opposing factions, competing nationalisms and simmering hatred.In June 1991, Croatia declared independence. Mladić was sent in with the Yugoslav army in an effort to re-impose control. He gained a reputation for courage bordering on recklessness, ever-present in frontline trenches and personally leading expeditions to clear mines. His men loved him for it, their devotion bordering on religious.As the war spilled over into Bosnia, his force switched uniforms - pledging support for the breakaway Republika Srpska. He saw the Muslim population as invaders - the result of an ancient occupation by Ottoman Turks.Image source, Corbis/Getty ImagesImage caption, A father kneels at his son's grave in SarajevoMladić vowed to right what he considered a historical injustice, drive out the intruders and then build the ethnically pure nation of his dreams.So began the siege of Sarajevo - the Bosnian capital defended by a rag-tag multi-ethnic force of Serbs, Croats and Bosniaks (Bosnian Muslims). With his troops dug in on surrounding hillsides, the blockade lasted 1,425 days. It was the longest city siege in the savage history of modern warfare.On 22 July 1993, nearly 4,000 shells rained down on its terrified people. By the end of the siege, 13,000 were dead from shell-fire or a sniper's bullet; almost every building in the city either damaged or destroyed. Image caption, Ratko Mladić (L) with Bosnian Serb leader Radovan KaradžićIn the villages around the capital, legions of men were killed or carted off to prison camps; thousands of women were mercilessly raped.A communiqué from Gen Mladić's headquarters captured his attitude. "Shoot at slow intervals until I order you to stop," it said. "Target Muslim neighbourhoods - not many Serbs live there. Shell them until they are on the edge of madness."Revelling in the power of his army, he gave orders by radio, the messages deliberately left unscrambled so they would be picked up and broadcast worldwide."Burn their brains," he screamed as his soldiers took aim at one enclave, telling them to follow his orders "as if given by God."Image source, Sygma via Getty ImagesImage caption, Emaciated prisoners at a Bosnian Serb camp in 1992. Later, some of the survivors would attend the trial of Ratko MladićAt weekends, he would visit his family, his wife and two children kept safe in Belgrade. They would play board games, the conversation deliberately avoiding politics. But his 23-year-old daughter, Ana, had fallen in love with a young doctor and human rights activist. The doctor gave her an ultimatum: renounce your father or never see me again.Torn between dreams of love and bonds of family, Ana took her father's favourite gun from its display case. Moments later, she pulled the trigger. Mladić struggled to come to terms with her suicide, preferring wild conspiracy theories which blamed the tragedy on everyone but himself.Finally, in 1995, Nato lost patience. It launched fighter attacks and cruise missile strikes on Mladić's positions around Sarajevo, most of them with devastating effect.  The siege was broken but his murderous campaign to cleanse the country was far from over.That summer, tens of thousands of Bosniak civilians were gathered in Srebrenica: a small mountain town in eastern Bosnia. They were under the protection of the United Nations, which had declared it a "safe area".Bosnian Serb troops bombarded them with heavy shells and rockets. Five days later, Mladić strutted into town surrounded by TV camera crews.Image source, Sygma via Getty ImagesImage caption, More than eight thousand men and boys were killed by troops in Srebrenica. The troops were under the command of General Mladić.In the main square, he handed out sweets, patted children on the head and assured them all would be fine. They were not fooled. The handful of Dutch peacekeepers did nothing as men were shot and women were raped.There followed the single most heinous act on European soil since World War Two. Mladić's troops rounded up every Bosniak male they could find, marched them to remote sites and murdered them on an industrial scale.In just a few days, 8,000 men and boys were tied up, blindfolded and shot. Some of them were as young as twelve, others in their late seventies. All of them were cruelly pushed into mass, unmarked graves.Image source, Gamma-Rapho Images via Getty ImagesImage caption, General Mladić leads his troops in 1994It was genocide: a black moment in European history and the UN's darkest hour. It was a crime that took a high degree of organisation; the people had been promised UN protection and all this had happened right under its nose.Later, the UN Secretary General, Kofi Annan, wrote that responsibility lay "first and foremost with those who planned and carried out the massacre". However, the international community had "made serious errors of judgement, rooted in a philosophy of impartiality", he added.Mladić was accused of war crimes. America offered $5m for information leading to his capture. A year later, Bosnian President Biljana Plavsic buckled to international pressure and dismissed him. Image source, Gamma-Rapho via Getty ImagesImage caption, Ratko Mladić is photographed in a military helicopter during the Bosnian War in 1994But it would be 14 years before he stood trial at the Hague.He returned to Belgrade, enjoying the support and protection of President Slobodan Milošević. Mladić lived openly; deer-hunting with friends, eating in swanky restaurants and even attending football matches.He remained a hero to swathes of his countrymen, who saw in him the Serbian martial spirit and an echo of the past glories of their nation. They were determined not to give him to an International Court. The president even established a military force dedicated to Mladić's personal protection.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Family members mourn a victim of the killings in Srebrenica. Many of the thousands left in unmarked graves were exhumed for proper burial.The net began to tighten when, in October 2000, Slobodan Milošević was himself arrested and later delivered to the Hague. International politics was beginning to bite, Serbia's entry to the European Union held up by its protection of the fugitives.That night, Mladić fled; no longer guaranteed the sanctuary of his state. He spent the next decade moving from safe-house to safe-house, first protected by a loyal team of bodyguards and, when they dwindled away, by his family.In July 2008, his former political ally, Radovan Karadžić - now a long-bearded faith-healer - was arrested on a bus in Belgrade. The new Serbian regime delivered him to the International Court, with which it had formalised co-operation. General Mladić was next.Three years later, he was found. The police tailed his children to a remote, squalid farmhouse where they stood alone in the courtyard for no apparent reason. Too nervous to meet them, Mladić was watching through a window. When the security forces went in, they found a dishevelled 69-year-old man who had suffered several strokes.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, An unrepentant Mladić gives a thumbs-up at his trial at the International Court of Justice at the HagueThe trial itself took four years. The court sat for more than 500 days, heard from nearly 600 witnesses, and examined nearly 10,000 bits of evidence. Due process was followed, although few doubted what the verdict would be.Ratko Mladić was shown giving orders to his troops immediately before the Srebrenica massacre and convicted of genocide, crimes against humanity and violations of the "customs of war".He entered the courtroom with a smile and a thumbs-up to the cameras but exploded with anger at the verdicts. Screaming that it was "all lies", he was forcibly removed. His sentence meant he would die in prison.Among the many victims and their relatives present at his trial was Fikret Alic, a prisoner famously filmed in a skeletal state in a Bosnian Serb concentration camp in 1992.  "Justice has been done," he said. "The war criminal has been convicted". Others simply dissolved in tears.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, A Sarajevo mural in 2023. Despite his crimes, Ratko Mladić remains popular with some Serbian nationalistsBut the widespread joy at the verdicts was far from universal. Some Bosniaks were disappointed he had not been convicted of crimes outside Sarajevo and Srebrenica. And many fellow Serbs reacted with rage.One leading politician in Republika Srpska condemned the trial as a plot to demonise his people, and called for them to "forever erase every mention" of the court proceedings from school history books.In 2024, the court turned down his application to serve the rest of his sentence in Serbia. Having suffered heart attacks and strokes, Mladić claimed that his health would be better protected in his home country. His lawyers continued to reapply unsuccessfully for his release, on the grounds that he had only months to live.Both Serbia and Russia have supported his legal appeals. In Bosnia, by contrast, an opposition politician was sentenced to three years in prison for "glorifying" Karadžić and Mladić in January 2026.For many of his people, the "Butcher of Bosnia" was just a simple soldier and the protector of their way of life. But he will be remembered by Bosniaks and most of the international community as a murderous thug who disgraced the European stage.In Bosnia, Muslims and Serbs live side-by-side in uneasy cohabitation. The violent nationalist war waged by Mladić and Radovan Karadžić  in the 1990s may be over, but tension still exists.

schema.headline: Ratko Mladić: The monstrous crimes of the 'Butcher of Bosnia'

title: UK salmonella cases nearing 500 as egg investigations continue
description: Close to 500 people have become ill with salmonella linked to imported eggs, say UK authorities, who say they have identified two new clusters of the
body: Close to 500 people have become ill with salmonella linked to imported eggs, say UK authorities, who say they have identified two new clusters of the infection.The UK Health Security Agency, external reported 207 cases last week. That has been increased to 259, with the two new clusters bringing the total to 474. There have been two deaths recorded.Some of the cases date back a year, but all involve bacteria that are almost genetically identical, suggesting a common food source.Investigations are ongoing, but based on what is known so far, experts say people have fallen sick after eating out rather than cooking eggs at home.Cases of salmonella are being seen in other European countries, external too - Austria (2), Belgium (15), Denmark (1), France (4), Germany (6), the Netherlands (106). Investigations in the Netherlands suggests a link with chicken meat, rather than eggs.Salmonella can be found in a number of food sources including raw or under-cooked poultry or meat and eggs.More than a third of those ill in the UK - some babies and others as old as 92 - have needed hospital care. Most people get better without treatment, however.While salmonella cases can happen any time, the UK outbreak involves a few specific, near-identical genetic clusters called t5.9411, t0.24068 and t5.9765.There have been:259 confirmed cases and one death linked to t5.941138 confirmed cases and one death linked to t5.9765177 confirmed cases linked to the t0.24068Most have been recorded in recent weeks and months, but the investigations go back to cases as far as August 2025. The majority have been in England, with many in London and Yorkshire and Humber.There have been a small number of cases in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland too.

schema.headline: UK salmonella cases nearing 500 as egg investigations continue

title: Nepal-Tibet floods: Survivors describe horror of loved ones being swept away
description: Survivors of massive flash floods in Nepal have recounted how they saw their loved ones disappear into torrents of mud.More than 175 people have died
body: Survivors of massive flash floods in Nepal have recounted how they saw their loved ones disappear into torrents of mud.More than 175 people have died and 800 others are missing after floods wiped out entire villages on the border of Nepal and Tibet on Wednesday, with a force so powerful seismologists initially identified it as an earthquake.Rescuers trudged through thick mud and debris on Thursday as Nepalese authorities rushed to bring aid and relief supplies to the affected areas."My family members were swept away by the flood in front of my eyes," Kalpana Malla from Nepal's Nuwakot district told the BBC.Malla said her father, mother, sister and sister's children were all claimed by the disaster."They could not escape the flood; there was no chance at all," she said. "This flood took everything, but my son and I climbed the rooftop of a house and survived but couldn't explain how."Her son, Sugam Malla, said he saved his mother by pulling her hand.He said he had given his phone to his sister so she could keep in touch, but the mobile was no longer reachable."I am worried she must be swept away."Another woman, Goma Pandit, said she had lost her buffaloes and all her other cattle."My farmland is also swept away. Ten sacks of mustard seeds, tons of corn and rice paddy are all gone. Nothing is left."At Kathmandu's TU Teaching Hospital, families of those missing in the floods wait anxiously for updates.Holding up her phone, Ram Khumari Shrestha says: "This is my husband. He was off to Rasuwa as a part of his driving job. He was in contact with me until 8 pm yesterday."But I couldn't call him this morning. The phone was switched off," she told the BBC.Mani Shrestha Bishwa was also camped out at the hospital on Wednesday night, hoping to hear from his younger brother, cousin, uncle and friend."I last contacted them at 8:30 in the morning," he said.Trekking guide Sonam Dorjee missed the flood in his home village of Rasiwa Syafru by about an hour. He had left at 08:00 local time.As he was driving to Kathmandu, Dorjee told the BBC he had heard the sound of floods gushing into their village."It [sounded] like an earthquake," he said. "My house has collapsed... I have seen a photo."Dorjee said his sister, Dechen Tamang, was missing, along with her husband and several other family members.He described the flood as "sudden and devastating"."Many survivors are now left without homes and they need emergency rescue and evacuation, as well as food, temporary accommodation and medical support."He is praying his sister is found alive. "There is a 10% chance, we hope," he said.

schema.headline: Nepal-Tibet floods: Survivors describe horror of loved ones being swept away

title: BBC director general Matt Brittin says he was not aware of 'severity' of cuts
description: During the conversation with Kirsty Wark, his first major industry appearance, Brittin also said he had been "impressed" by the "creativity and talent
body: During the conversation with Kirsty Wark, his first major industry appearance, Brittin also said he had been "impressed" by the "creativity and talent" at the BBC, but added "every media organisation is struggling with rapidly changing consumer behaviour and the power of the AI revolution".Describing the corporation as "inward looking", he also criticised the organisation for this leading to "an aversion to risk"."You've got very loud critics, many of whom are the commercial rivals of the corporation and you've got political pressure on everything that you do journalistically," he said.Brittin, who previously worked at Google, took over from Tim Davie earlier this year.He is the first director-general since Greg Dyke in 2000 to take on the role having not been a former BBC employee. The former regional policy manager for the tech giant said he wanted to use those skills to "move faster through experimenting and learning" at the organisation and work with colleagues to "find a way to the future together".Brittin also spoke about the BBC's need to "defend its integrity" as it challenges Donald Trump's defamation case.The US president is seeking $10bn (£7.4bn) in damages in a Florida court over the editing of a Panorama documentary from 2024 about the US Capitol riots.Legal representatives for the BBC are looking to have the case thrown out, and the corporation has previously apologised for an "error of judgement" in the editing of the programme."We moved to dismiss the case on the grounds of jurisdiction in that nobody in the US actually saw the show with the bad edits, and it was a bad edit, and he won the election, and he's got richer," Brittin said during the conversation.

schema.headline: BBC director general Matt Brittin says he was not aware of 'severity' of cuts

title: Ratko Mladić: BBC correspondent on meeting dangerous fanatic early in Bosnian war
description: Bosnian Serb commander Ratko Mladić, dubbed the "Butcher of Bosnia" for his actions during the Balkan wars of the 1990s, has died in prison.BBC specia
body: Bosnian Serb commander Ratko Mladić, dubbed the "Butcher of Bosnia" for his actions during the Balkan wars of the 1990s, has died in prison.BBC special correspondent Allan Little was there throughout the breakup of the former Yugoslavia, and met Mladić in the early months of the Bosnian war.At night, you could watch the fires of ethnic cleansing across the landscape. The flames provided the only light under the night sky and the black valley would glimmer with flecks of orange.You could watch the men of our village move about silently in the shadows of their homes, each armed with some ancient weapon salvaged from wars long ago and, like the fears and the suspicions and the distrusts, handed down through the generations.One morning I watched a procession of men and women emerge from a forest. They had been driven from their homes two days earlier and had fled with what they could carry.Most were on foot. Some were crammed into the back of ancient farm vehicles drawn by donkeys. There were perhaps 40,000 of them. Their home town had fallen to a Serb advance that had come without warning.Among them, one man seemed close to collapse. He stopped to speak to us.The whole town had fled, he said. He had become separated from his wife in the long trek to safety and was now worried that she had not made it. His pale, almost translucently white skin was stretched across the bones of his face like parchment. His forehead was livid blue from a fall.I asked him how old he was. He said he was 80. "May I ask" I said, "are you a Croat or a Muslim?"The memory of it shames me even now as I hear, in my mind, his answer echo down the years."I am," he said, "a musician".Our convenient ethnic shorthand reduced them to Serbs, Croats and Muslims. But they were also musicians and scientists and doctors and plumbers and farmers and mothers and fathers and brothers and sisters and very often children.I met Mladić in that first hot summer of the war in Bosnia. We were at Lukavica barracks on the southern edge of Sarajevo. The barracks was awash with weapons and the menacing strut of the paramilitaries. You could buy a Kalashnikov for 200 dollars, a hand grenade for just one dollar – the same price, I would soon learn, as the cost of a fresh egg in the besieged city.I shook his hand and he held it fast and pulled me in close. He told me he had just come back from the Sarajevo city centre front line and I saw that he was pumped up by the exhilarating proximity of the fighting.He held my hand for many minutes, fixed me with his eye and told me he was the great defender of brotherhood and unity in former Yugoslavia, and that he dreamed of a world in which there would no guns and no war. He struck me then as fanatical, dangerously so.In the years that lay ahead, forces under his command committed the worst war crimes on European soil since the Nazis. They bequeathed to the lexicon of war a grim new euphemism - ethnic cleansing. They committed mass murder, extermination, mass rape, forced expulsions. They burned village after village, all in the name of creating an ethnically put Serbian territory in Croatia and Serbia. Ultimately, at Srebrenica, they committed genocide.Two days after I had met the old musician on that damp muddy roadside, I found myself drawn into the passions of the war in a personal and – at the time – devastating way. My cameraman, Tihomir Tunukovic, a man I had known and worked alongside during the previous 18 months, was killed by a Serb gunner on a ridge above the road he was driving on. We had parted earlier that morning. He was 25 years old, a talented and ambitious young film maker from Zagreb. We drove his body back along the rutted mountain pathways to the coastal city of Split. We broke our hearts at his funeral. The grief of it connected us to the sentiments of the war – the impulse to vengeance and counter vengeance – that were so much a feature of what we were witnessing.General Mladić did not pull the trigger but his command created an atmosphere of wanton permissiveness which cost tens of thousands of lives.

schema.headline: Ratko Mladić: BBC correspondent on meeting dangerous fanatic early in Bosnian war

title: What we should make of CIA boss John Ratcliffe’s secret trip to Moscow
description: One US official told Politico that the "meeting was primarily to warn Russia against any escalatory action against the Baltic states".The UK is also i
body: One US official told Politico that the "meeting was primarily to warn Russia against any escalatory action against the Baltic states".The UK is also in Russian crosshairs. On Thursday, a foreign ministry spokeswoman said Russia could strike British military targets as retaliation for Ukrainian strikes on Russia using British missiles.And a drone carrying an explosive which was discovered at an airport in the German city of Leipzig was probably Russian, security experts have said.News of Ratcliffe's visit follows reports of US intelligence assessments that President Vladimir Putin was planning a limited assault on a Nato ally.But you don't need the world's most powerful electronic eavesdropping organisation – the US National Security Agency – to know that Putin is under mounting domestic pressure to "do something" to break the deadlock.Ukraine's deep strikes with long-range drones have not only hammered Russia's energy industry, they have brought the war home to ordinary Russians.Nothing says things are not going to plan more than long queues for petrol and billowing smoke coming from stricken oil refineries. The Kremlin sees these attacks as Nato fighting an indirect war on Russia by using Ukraine as a proxy.So how will Russia respond? There is a broad spectrum of possibilities here.These include stepping up the ballistic missile attacks on Ukraine that Moscow is already launching, including targeting the centre of Kyiv, knowing that Ukraine is running dangerously low on Patriot interceptors to stop them.Putin will be well aware of Donald Trump's periodic disdain for Nato and he may have calculated that a low-key attack on say, Lithuania, is not going to trigger Nato's mutual self-defence clause – Article 5 – and that the US will not respond.In which case it would make sense for part of the CIA chief's unexplained mission to Moscow was to remind Russia that the US is still fully committed to Article 5.Lithuania is of special interest to the Kremlin as it has a common border with Poland known as the "Suwalki Gap". Just 60 miles long, this strip of land is all that separates Russia's client state Belarus from its nuclear-armed exclave of Kaliningrad, which is separated from mainland Russia.If Russia were to seize that it would effectively cut off those three Baltic states by land from their Nato neighbours.Then there is the question of tactical nuclear warheads. It has long been said that Russian military doctrine views these small but highly destructive weapons as an integral part of its order of battle.Moscow has been warned off, by friend and foe alike, not to break the 81-year long taboo on using nuclear weapons in anger.Yet this could still be a tempting option for Vladimir Putin to "escalate to de-escalate" by demonstrating to Ukraine that it has such catastrophic weapons at its disposal it would be better for Kyiv to capitulate to Moscow's terms now or face annihilation.Of course, in the absence of any clear, attributable, official confirmation from the US as to what this sudden CIA dash to Moscow was all about then it is always possible it was about something else.That could be trying to persuade Russia to end its military cooperation with Iran, for example, or maybe about more prisoner swaps or the prospect of a mass mobilisation of Russian troops.But make no mistake, this trip was highly unusual and it came at a time of rising tension between Moscow and the West. Something is almost certainly up.

schema.headline: What we should make of CIA boss John Ratcliffe’s secret trip to Moscow

title: Dame Jenni Murray died days after car crash, inquest hears
description: BBC broadcaster Dame Jenni Murray died days after being involved in a car crash in which she was dazzled by headlights, an inquest was told.Dame Jenni
body: BBC broadcaster Dame Jenni Murray died days after being involved in a car crash in which she was dazzled by headlights, an inquest was told.Dame Jenni, who was the longest-serving presenter of BBC Radio 4's Woman's Hour, died aged 75 on 12 March, eight days after a collision in north London. North London area coroner Tony Murphy ruled her cause of death was bronchopneumonia caused by fractures to her rib and sternum fractures sustained in the crash.A statement from Dr Clare Morkane,  a consultant at the Royal Free Hospital where Dame Jenni died after being admitted on 4 March, stated: "Jennifer had been driving when she became dazzled by vehicle lights and collided with two stationary vehicles."Dr Morkane added: "Following the collision, Jennifer was unable to recall events, exited the vehicle independently and she was conveyed to hospital."The crash took place near Hampstead Heath, at around 19:45 GMT, the inquest heard.It resulted in "multiple rib fractures", a fracture to the upper sternum and a collapsed lung.The broadcaster was initially placed on non-invasive ventilation before being moved to intensive care, but she developed bronchopneumonia.The Metropolitan Police investigated the crash but closed its investigation with no further action.Dame Jenni joined Woman's Hour in 1987 and left in 2020.Vintage moments from the shows she presented included a confrontation with Baroness Margaret Thatcher about her childcare policies, a flirtatious interview with actor Jack Nicholson, challenging Edwina Currie about her affair with then PM John Major, and asking Hillary Clinton how she could forgive her husband Bill's infidelity.Other highlights included an interview with her favourite singer Joan Baez - "the peak of my career", she once said.After her death was announced, the then-BBC director general Tim Davie paid tribute to her as "a broadcasting icon", while Radio 4 controller Mohit Bakaya described her as "warm, fearless and beloved by listeners".Dame Jenni announced on air in 2006 that she had been diagnosed with breast cancer.As well as speaking to her listeners about her breast cancer diagnosis, she also spoke openly about her weight loss surgery and the menopause.In 2011, she received a damehood in recognition of her contribution to broadcasting, and also won two Sony Awards and was made a member of the Radio Academy Hall of Fame during her career.

schema.headline: Dame Jenni Murray died days after car crash, inquest hears

title: Top Gear to return after Andrew Flintoff's crash, BBC confirms
description: Image caption, Speedy driver The Stig has always been a key part of the showByIan YoungsCulture reporterUpdated 7 hours agoTop Gear is to return to TV
body: Image caption, Speedy driver The Stig has always been a key part of the showByIan YoungsCulture reporterUpdated 7 hours agoTop Gear is to return to TV, the BBC has confirmed, four years after the show was "rested" when co-host Andrew Flintoff was injured in a crash during filming.The long-running motoring programme has been off air since 2022, when the former cricketer suffered serious facial and rib injuries when his open-topped three-wheeled car overturned at the show's test track.He was one of three presenters at the time along with Paddy McGuinness and Chris Harris.The hosting line-up for the comeback has not yet been announced, although the Sun newspaper last week reported that comedian Jimmy Carr was in talks to join.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The BBC's director of entertainment said Jimmy Carr "would be a great host but I won't be discussing that today"The BBC's director of entertainment Ed Havard told the Edinburgh TV Festival on Thursday: "There has been a lot of speculation about this and we can confirm that Top Gear is coming back."I'm not going to talk about talent today."Asked whether Jimmy Carr would be hosting, he replied: "Jimmy would be a great host but I won't be discussing that today."We will have more information on Top Gear shortly."Former rugby player and Celebrity Traitors star Joe Marler is also reportedly in the frame to host.The show will be made by BBC Studios, which did not comment further.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Andrew Flintoff, Paddy McGuinness and Chris Harris hosted the show before it was restedTop Gear began in 1977 and became one of the BBC's biggest hits in the hands of Jeremy Clarkson, Richard Hammond and James May in the 2000s.They were replaced by broadcaster Chris Evans and Friends star Matt LeBlanc, before Flintoff, McGuinness and Harris took over in 2018.The BBC apologised and paid compensation to Flintoff following his crash.He has described being dragged face-down underneath the Morgan Super 3 car for about 50 metres. "I thought I was dead," he told a Disney+ documentary last year.Paul Rees, a racing driver and expert adviser who was in the car with Flintoff, has sued BBC Studios for up to £150,000 for personal injury. BBC Studios has said: "We dispute this claim and are defending it."

schema.headline: Top Gear to return after Andrew Flintoff's crash, BBC confirms

title: What does the Meta settlement mean for the UK? Five things we learned
description: The UK has its own measures in place to protect children online.The Online Safety Act mainly put restrictions on what content young people can see onl
body: The UK has its own measures in place to protect children online.The Online Safety Act mainly put restrictions on what content young people can see online.But the UK government has gone further than the US ban already.Earlier this year, it announced an outright social media ban for under-16s, which will take effect in 2027.Some other measures will apply to 16 and 17-year-olds, such as curfews and restrictions during certain hours of the day.The US has to some extent followed the same path: Start by policing the content on the platforms, then move on to restricting access to social media.But the core difference is children in the US will not be banned completely.Instead, they will not have access to Facebook and Instagram overnight, have to follow time limits, and there will be prompts for children who use them for a long time.Unlike in the UK, these are not put in by law, and will only apply to the two platforms so far (more on that below).The UK government said it was "following developments closely" in the Meta settlement.But now those safety features have been accepted by Meta in the US, other countries may start asking for them too."These tech platforms don't usually do anything unless they are told to do it," said Trevor Johnson, a former senior figure at Meta and TikTok, who spoke to Radio 4's Today programme."But I do think the UK will feel empowered to at least ask for the same restrictions."Another former Meta director, Zvika Krieger, said Meta agreed to the changes because it saw "the writing on the wall"."They're trying to demonstrate, 'Oh, you don't need to go and do a complete ban'," he told 5 Live Breakfast."I think that they probably would roll out a lot of these features to the rest of the world as well."Meta may have been the target in this court case, but it has tried to bring the rest of Big Tech into the firing line.At the same time as announcing the settlement, Meta called on TikTok and YouTube to bring in the same measures.A Meta spokesperson told Reuters the company was "hopeful" Snap would make similar changes too.The tech firm has always argued for a level playing field when it comes to regulation - it doesn't want Facebook and Instagram to be more restricted than its rivals, which might be able to hoover up teens who want a freer experience online."All platforms should empower parents and support teens in these ways because we know that when teens are restricted on one app, they simply move to another," Meta said.YouTube, Snapchat and TikTok have maintained they have robust children's safety policies in place."There will be pressure for those platforms to adopt similar restrictions," Johnson said.But they may not come willingly. So far, almost 24 hours after the gauntlet was thrown down by Meta, none have made a public comment."Time and time again social media companies don't make changes until they're forced," Ellen Roome, whose son Jools died after taking part in an online challenge, told Today.Roome is part of a group of parents suing TikTok in the US over child safety.Meta will pay out up to $18bn to almost all US states, plus the District of Columbia and three US territories.30% of that is dependent on TikTok and YouTube agreeing to put in child safety measures.This is far less than the hundreds of billions being speculated ahead of the trial.It is also a fraction of Meta's revenue of $201bn last year - and Meta will be paying out the money over the course of a decade.But the firm's future revenue may be affected by a drop in users or younger users spending less time on their platforms.The complainants will share the money, with different states getting different amounts - but they will get hundreds of millions of dollars each.New York state, which will receive at least $819m according to its attorney general, said the money would be used "to support mental health services, education programs, and other efforts to repair and reduce the harm caused by unhealthy social media use among young people".Many other states have said they have earmarked the cash for similar initiatives.The only two US states not included are Florida, which rejected the settlement, and New Mexico, which was not included in the offer after a previous court cases resulted in a $942m fine.Former Meta whistleblower Arturo Béjar, who was a witness in the trial, cited the now-familiar comparison of social media with Big Tobacco.But, he told the BBC, even after companies were found to be pushing harmful products, they "were still able to sell cigarettes and the cigarettes were still as harmful".Alexa Knight from the Mental Health Foundation gave a different analogy - consumer products."We expect the manufacturers to make sure their products are safe before they're released... particularly when there are children using them," she told 5 Live Breakfast. "And we think it should be the same way for Big Tech."That is to say, campaigners like Béjar and Knight are not going away.Roome also said the new measures in place were a start, but don't go far enough.There will be time limits on app usage, she said, "but what about the content on the platform?" No one is claiming the settlement is a silver bullet, but it's likely Meta and its fellow social media companies will continue to face scrutiny over the safety of children and adults on its platforms.

schema.headline: What does the Meta settlement mean for the UK? Five things we learned

title: Champions League draw: Champions Paris St-Germain to face Manchester City and Aston Villa
description: European champions Paris St-Germain will face Premier League duo Manchester City and Aston Villa as well as five-time winners Barcelona in the league
body: European champions Paris St-Germain will face Premier League duo Manchester City and Aston Villa as well as five-time winners Barcelona in the league phase of this season's Champions League. The back-to-back Champions League winners will welcome Barca to Parc des Princes, while they were also handed trips to Villa Park and Manchester in the draw for the league phase. Premier League champions Arsenal, meanwhile, will host 15-time winners Real Madrid at Emirates Stadium, and have also been handed a trip to Bayern Munich. Mikel Arteta's men, who were beaten by PSG on penalties in the final last season, will face Borussia Dortmund, Real Betis, Lille, Napoli, Azerbaijan champions Sabah and Slavia Prague as well.Enzo Maresca's City will welcome PSG to Etihad Stadium and travel to Barcelona, where they will have a reunion with Spanish World Cup-winner Rodri, who moved to the Nou Camp in a £65m deal this summer. City will also be up against another of their former midfielders in Kevin de Bruyne when Napoli visit Manchester, with Sporting, Porto, RB Leipzig, AEK Athens and Lens their other opponents.Europa League winners Villa, returning to the competition after a season away, will host PSG and Dortmund and travel to Barcelona and Galatasaray. Unai Emery's side also face Club Brugge, Fenerbahce, Viking and Slavia Prague.Manchester United, returning after a two-year hiatus, will meet Bayern, Atletico Madrid, Roma, Sporting, Leipzig, Villarreal, Sabah and Como.Liverpool, meanwhile, host Atletico, Porto, Villarreal and Lens while visiting Inter Milan, Brugge, Fenerbahce and LASK.The first league-phase matches will be played on Tuesday, 8 September and the last round of games will take place on 27 January 2027, with the exact schedule to be released on Saturday.This season's final will be held in Madrid on 5 June.Arsenal: Real Madrid (home), Bayern Munich (away), Borussia Dortmund (home), Real Betis (away), Lille (home), Napoli (away), Sabah (home), Slavia Prague (away)Aston Villa: PSG (home), Barcelona (away), Borussia Dortmund (home), Club Brugge (away), Fenerbahce (home), Galatasaray (away), Viking (home), Slavia Prague (away)Liverpool: Atletico Madrid (home), Inter Milan (away), Porto (home), Club Brugge (away), Villarreal (home), Fenerbahce (away), Lens (home), LASK (away)Manchester City: PSG (home), Barcelona (away), Sporting Club (home), Porto (away), Napoli (home), Leipzig (away), AEK Athens (home), Lens (away)Manchester United: Bayern Munich (home), Atletico Madrid (away), Roma (home), Sporting Club (away), Leipzig (home), Villarreal (away), Sabah (home), Como (away)Each of the 36 teams plays eight different teams - four at home and four away - in the league phase.Teams who finish in the top eight automatically qualify for the last 16, while those placing ninth to 24th will compete in a two-legged knockout play-off for the chance to join them.Sides who finish 25th or lower will be eliminated, and will not drop into the Europa League.Last season, eventual runners-up Arsenal topped the league phase standings with 24 points after eight wins from as many matches. Liverpool were third - behind second-placed Bayern Munich - with 18 points while Tottenham finished one point behind in fourth.Chelsea and Manchester City also qualified directly for the last 16 after finishing sixth and eighth respectively while Newcastle finished 12th.Chelsea, Manchester City, Newcastle and Spurs were knocked out in the last 16 last season while Liverpool were beaten in the quarter-finals by PSG, who also edged Arsenal in the final for their second consecutive title.Watch highlights of every Champions League game from 22:00 on Wednesday on BBC iPlayer and the BBC Sport website and app.There will also be a Champions League Match of the Day on BBC One on Wednesday, from 22:40 to 00:00.

title: King Charles 'heartbroken' by deadly Nepal flash floods
description: The King says he and Queen Camilla are "heartbroken" by the deadly flash floods near the Nepal-Tibet border, as 33 people from the UK are missing incl
body: The King says he and Queen Camilla are "heartbroken" by the deadly flash floods near the Nepal-Tibet border, as 33 people from the UK are missing including a 13-year-old girl and 14-year-old boy.The Prince and Princess of Wales also expressed their shock, saying they were "thinking of everyone caught up in this terrible disaster".The death toll from the floods has risen to at least 359, with more than 1,300 people missing, 644 of whom are tourists according to Nepali authorities.Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the UK has offered £5m to help the Nepalese government following the floods, adding it was a "very distressing and devastating situation".King Charles said that he and the Queen were sending their "most profound sympathy to all those who have so tragically lost their loved ones"."Many in the United Kingdom have strong, deep and personal ties to this part of the world," the King's statement continued."We feel deeply for the many families awaiting anxiously the news of friends and relations."Our hearts go out also to the families of all the police and armed forces personnel who lost their lives while carrying out their courageous duty in the service of others."The prime minister and the Foreign Office in the UK have urged people to follow local guidance and remain alert to the changing situation, as officials in Nepal warn of a possible secondary flood risk near the Bhote Koshi river.The Foreign Office added it was working closely with Nepalese authorities.British resident Pramod Pudel, who lives in East Sussex but is originally from Nepal, told BBC Radio Sussex on Thursday that "nothing remains" where his family lives and he is flying back to search for his wife, mother, brother and uncle."It's a very, very difficult time for me and for my family and my country at this moment, but obviously I have to go and see what's happening there," he said."A lot of people are missing and there is no information regarding who is missing, where they are. Nobody can contact each other and all the bridges are broken, so you can't cross the land."There's no power, no electricity, so I can't contact anyone, so it's a very difficult time not knowing what's happening."Tour companies including Alpine Eco Trek, The Trekkers' Society, Himalayan Glacier US, Kailash Journeys and Fishtail Tours have reported missing British nationals while on trips with the companies.Alpine Eco Trek said it has not been able to establish contact with 12 Britons who were booked on a tour to Mount Kailash and were in the region when the flash floods struck.The company's travel logs which were shared with the Press Association, with a 13-year-old girl the youngest person missing.Four of the firm's Nepali tour guides are also missing.Mount Kailash - a peak in the Himalayas near the border between Nepal and Tibet - is considered the spiritual home of the Hindu god Shiva.The journey to the mountain is part of the Kailash Mansarovar Yatra, a sacred pilgrimage for Hindus. The pilgrimage had only recently resumed after being disrupted first by the pandemic and then by tensions between India and China.The Trekkers' Society said nine UK nationals on a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash are missing after they crossed the Nepal-Tibet border. Four males aged between 14 and 50, and five females aged 40 to 53 remain missing.Himalayan Glacier US had 47 guests on a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, with two in the group being British citizens.Kailash Journeys reported 27 guests and staff were missing, with two British men in the group. Fishtail Tours said one British person on its tour was missing.The flood hit early on Wednesday in Rasuwa, just north of Nepal's capital Kathmandu.Preliminary information suggested it was caused by an earthquake, but the US Geological Survey said additional analysis indicated "the seismic energy was instead generated by a landslide."It said a magnitude 5.2 seismic event caused by a "glacial collapse and debris flow" occurred near the border at 08:37 local time on Wednesday.

schema.headline: King Charles 'heartbroken' by deadly Nepal flash floods

title: France relaxes strict cheese-making rules after prolonged drought
description: The National Institute for Origin and Quality (INAO), which regulates France's labels of origin, has also approved temporary changes to the rules for
body: The National Institute for Origin and Quality (INAO), which regulates France's labels of origin, has also approved temporary changes to the rules for other protected produce because of the effects of the summer heat.Products that will benefit include some types of Calvados and cider from Normandy, Crémant d'Alsace fizzy wine, lamb from Poitou-Charentes,  and Reine-Claude plums.Certificates of origin allow farmers to sell at a premium, but they come with strict regulations governing the location and method of production. The aim is to preserve the unique identity of cheeses, wines and other foodstuffs, supposedly linked to their particular terroir - a French concept that links locality and tradition.Because of a 2026 drought - which the INAO now describes as "historic" - farmers are being allowed to bend the rules for a short period.Makers of Abondance cheese in the Alps, for example, will be authorised to reduce the amount of pastured grass in their animals' diet from 50%  to 15%.  They will be entitled to import forage from outside their zone, and use some supplements.Makers of Comté cheese in the Jura mountains will be able to replace the local green maize they usually give to their cattle with maize from elsewhere.The derogations are allowed in French and European law for periods of exceptional weather. Similar measures came in after the dry summer of 2022.It will be interesting to see if the changes lead to any detectable change in the taste or quality of the cheeses - or to the quantity produced and how it is priced.Longer term,  the measures raise questions over the viability of the existing labels of origin in France and elsewhere.  If changing climate means that certain foodstuffs can no longer be produced in their traditional localities, then the idea of terroir will be stretched to its limits.

schema.headline: France relaxes strict cheese-making rules after prolonged drought

title: Dolly Parton biopic, coffee brand and dog treats among star's upcoming business projects
description: Nozell said that Parton had worked with her "handpicked" team for the past several years, to "build a project roadmap that will guide us for decades t
body: Nozell said that Parton had worked with her "handpicked" team for the past several years, to "build a project roadmap that will guide us for decades to come". The hugely successful and popular singer-songwriter and philanthropist took shrewd decisions throughout her career, which made her millions. Just before her death, she told People on 21 August she was exploring new ways of touring, and that her team was collaborating with companies that create "avatar performances", external given her recent health concerns.She added they were in the "early stages of development", People said.Other upcoming projects include:Dolly's Tennessean Travel Stops (celebrating National Truck Driver Appreciation Week)Dolly Parton's SongTeller HotelDolly scripted seriesDocuseriesBilly the Kid animated seriesDolly DollsDolly's Life of Many Colors MuseumDolly's Cup Of Ambition CoffeeDolly's Dog TreatsDolly on the HollyDolly Bedding & Home Decor Her Broadway show, Dolly: A True Original Musical, opens in December. Harry Styles added his voice to the deluge of tributes for Parton, saying at his Madison Square Garden show she was "inspiration to his career". He also included her song I Will Always Love you, external as part of his show. Meanwhile, flags across the US flew at half-mast on Wednesday, in tribute to the singer. A family source has told news outlets that a private funeral service is due to take place this weekend in Nashville.Last year, Parton said she had one song she couldn't talk about - it was still secret and buried in a vault in Dollywood, external, and will not be released until 2045."It's not supposed to be open 'til I'll be 100, and which, that's the day after tomorrow," Parton joked at the time.

title: England vs Pakistan: Jamie Smith and Jordan Cox battle in second Test at Lord's
description: Smith & Cox help England to 248-9 on truncated day oneFigure caption, Watch the moment Cox is dismissed by Salman Agha's 'unbelievable' catchByCricket
body: Smith & Cox help England to 248-9 on truncated day oneFigure caption, Watch the moment Cox is dismissed by Salman Agha's 'unbelievable' catchByCricket Correspondent at Lord'sUpdated 43 minutes agoSecond Rothesay Test, Lord's (day one of five)England 248-9: Smith 61, Cox 55; Abbas 4-56Pakistan: Yet to batScorecardJamie Smith and Jordan Cox battled difficult conditions and an improved Pakistan performance to take England to a competitive total on the opening day of the second Test.In the damp and gloom at Lord's, Smith made 61 and Cox 55 to take England to 248-9 on a first day that was delayed by rain and curtailed by bad light.The value of the hosts' score will only be revealed in time. The Lord's pitch is much better than the poor surface used for England's win against New Zealand in June, while more rain is forecast for the next three days.It could be that England have batted themselves into a position from where they can win this match and the series, which would be a successful end to a troubling week dominated by the Brydon Carse controversy.Cox was again impressive in only his third Test. He added 67 for the for sixth wicket with Smith, who looked fluent for a much-needed half-century.England were boosted by a late cameo of 34 not out from Gus Atkinson, while Pakistan were led by four wickets from Muhammad Abbas and three from Mohammad Ali. Things could have better for the tourists had they not dropped three catches.Under a dark sky and with the floodlights on, England would probably have wanted to bowl before the day was out, only for the light to end proceedings.England battle on the field after tough week off itFigure caption, 'He's holding England together' - Cox brings up his 50For England, the chance to win their first Test series since 2024 comes after yet another off-field drinking incident.Carse was removed from the squad for this Test after a night out in Derby on Saturday, with police investigating allegations of an assault. Carse is in the Durham side for their ongoing County Championship match against Gloucestershire.The home side steamrollered Pakistan at Headingley in Joe Root's first Test back as captain. It was always likely Pakistan would improve on their performance from Leeds, simply because the tourists could not play much worse.Pakistan were boosted by the return of captain Babar Azam from a hand injury, in the side for Salman Ali Agha who skippered in Leeds. Babar's first impact was to call correctly and play finally got under way at 12:20 BST.The tourists' trio of fast-medium seamers were ideally suited to the conditions and they showed much greater control than last week.England were sometimes wasteful - Dan Lawrence ran himself out and Harry Brook was bowled driving - and sometimes unlucky - Emilio Gay was caught down the leg side. For the most part, the batters were happy to roll up their sleeves, another encouraging sign early in Root's second reign.The result was a compelling contest, an arm wrestle with neither side ever able to claim they held the upper hand.England's total seems at least workable, yet Pakistan have the chance to gain a foothold if they bat well. This could turn into a tight Test.Cox and Smith impress for EnglandFigure caption, Best shots - Smith hits 61 to help England fight back on day oneCox is already showing himself to be difficult to leave out once Jacob Bethell returns from a knee injury, and one way England could retain him would be as wicketkeeper ahead of Smith.On this occasion, they combined for the two telling batting contributions of the day, albeit in contrasting styles.Abbas did the damage to the top order, with Root once again lbw with the keeper up to the stumps. When Lawrence was run out in a mix-up with Cox, England were 120-5 and teetering.By this point, Cox had once again shown he has the technique and temperament for the highest level - he was patient as Pakistan dried up the scoring immediately after lunch.Smith was given a life on 15 when keeper Mohammad Rizwan completely missed an edge off Ali. Reprieved, he dominated the strike and scoring in the stand with Cox, forcing the ball through the covers and whipping off his pads.It took a moment of magic to part them. Salman, on as a sub, flew to his right at second slip to hold Cox, one-handed, off Khurram Shahzad.Pakistan improve but could have been betterFigure caption, Gay goes after Rizwan's stunning 'Superman' catchThis was an opportunity for Pakistan to get back into the series. Had England won the toss it feels reasonable to suspect the home bowlers would have made life very difficult for the fragile visiting batting.Abbas was magnificent. At one point he claimed three wickets for four runs in the space of 16 balls - Gay, Ben Duckett and Root.He received support from Ali, whose three wickets were all batters bowled by the ball nipping down the Lord's slope. Brook, Smith and Ollie Robinson were his victims.Two of Pakistan's drops did not prove too costly. Root was missed at third slip by Imam-ul-Haq on one, though the skipper was out for four. Shan Masood spilled a simple catch at mid-wicket when Lawrence had 10, then the same fielder made amends to run out Lawrence for 17.Rizwan's miss was the most costly, symptomatic of the keeper and slip fielders appearing to stand too deep for most of the day with a number of edges not carrying through.

schema.headline: England vs Pakistan: Jamie Smith and Jordan Cox battle in second Test at Lord's

title: What we know about deadly Nepal-Tibet floods
description: Figure caption, Video shows scale of flash flood hitting Nepal-Tibet borderByOlivia Ireland and Henry MooreUpdated 8 hours agoMassive landslides and f
body: Figure caption, Video shows scale of flash flood hitting Nepal-Tibet borderByOlivia Ireland and Henry MooreUpdated 8 hours agoMassive landslides and flash floods on the Nepal-Tibet border have caused widespread damage and left hundreds dead or missing.Search and rescue operations are under way. Chinese state media has said there are significant casualties, while Nepalese officials anticipate "huge scale loss".Here is what we know so far.Image source, Nepal Army via EPAImage caption, Military teams were brought in to help with rescue and evacuation following the flooding on WednesdayWhat caused the deadly landslide?Nepal's foreign minister initially said an earthquake was reported on the Tibet-Nepal border shortly before the landslide, suggesting it may have triggered the disaster.The United States Geological Survey (USGS) had first reported the event as a magnitude 4.4 earthquake on Wednesday, but later confirmed the incident "was instead a glacial collapse and debris flow" that "caused subsequent catastrophic impacts downstream"."Additional analysis of nearby seismic stations, long period seismic waves, and satellite imagery led to the determination that the seismic event was instead a glacial collapse and debris flow, and that no earthquake had occurred," USGS said on Thursday.Earlier Nepali authorities had also told the BBC that a massive chunk of ice may have collapsed from a mountain, pulling down rocks and other sediments with it.Climate change is known to be driving faster glacier melt in the Hindu Kush Himalaya region and, as rescue efforts continue, scientists are trying to piece together the exact order of events.Simon Cook, senior lecturer in energy environment and security at the University of Dundee who specialises in glaciology, said "climate change could have an impact".Cook said his team had detected that the lower part of a glacier in Nepal near the Langtang Lirung peak - which is approximately 15km (9 miles) west of the site of the floods - had collapsed.Figure caption, He estimated that the glacier collapsed in a northwesterly direction and then travelled westwards downstream.He told the BBC "permafrost is partially holding some mountainsides together, this permafrost is warming and thawing and degrading so you are going to get more landslides".Mike Searle, professor of Earth sciences at Oxford University, said the glacier could have collapsed "hours or days" before the flooding hit Nepal and Tibet. He told the BBC: "I think the sheer wave of debris suggests there was a landslide first, the water built up, (which) dammed the river, and then it burst in one huge great flood."One possibility is that water from rainfall or melting ice may have destabilised the ground or ice, triggering a chain reaction.Scientist will be looking at satellite images of exactly where the landslide occurred, whether any glacial lakes suddenly drained, and where the river might have become blocked, as well as data on recent rainfall.A deluge of material careered towards northern Nepalese towns, including areas popular with mountaineering tourists and pilgrims. The border is around 40 miles (64.4km) north of Nepal's capital city Kathmandu. Footage showed a wall of mud and rock sweeping away buildings, roads and vehicles, as people fled the fast-moving wave of material in the Nuwakot region.In one video, a towering wall of water and mud was seen rushing down a gorge along the Trishuli River and enveloping the Rasuvagadhi Border check point, a multi-storey building.Severe flooding has been reported along the Bhote Koshi, Trishuli and Narayani rivers.Deaths have also been reported in villages on the Tibetan side of the border.The International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIDMOD) has warned secondary flooding could occur in the coming days as a result of the debris that washed into the river systems.In a report, the ICIDMOD said they are in the process of assessing whether the Trishuli River has been temporarily blocked in narrow sections. If it has been blocked, it is at risk of forming a landslide dam - and a second flooding event.Authorities and scientists are continuing to evaluate the size, location and stability of any potential blockages.Figure caption, Watch: BBC Nepali's Shreejana Shrestha is at a hospital in Kathmandu, where some survivors are being flown in by helicopterHow many people are dead and missing?The number of people killed or missing is still becoming clear Nepali police say at least 359 people have died. Among those killed, 64 were found in downstream areas in the Chitwan district while another 26 were found in Nawalparasi East. In an update on Thursday morning, Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said 826 people are still missing, including more than 529 tourists, with 466 foreigners among them.Meanwhile, China's state broadcaster CCTV said on Thursday that the number of people missing in the mudslide disaster in Tibet's Gyirong county had risen to 558.Among these are 260 foreign nationals, CCTV said, adding that the death toll remained at three.The Nepal Tourism Board said on Thursday that 644 tourists are still missing, 33 of which are UK nationals. It is not clear if any of the missing in the Nepali and Chinese figures have been counted twice.The border at Gyirong is the main crossing point for tourists and traffic between China and Nepal.Image source, ReutersHow are governments responding?Nepal's prime minister said "the entire nation has been left shocked and deeply distressed" and that officials would coordinate with China on the response. China's President Xi Jinping urged an "all-out" search effort, and promised stronger monitoring and early warning systems to prevent secondary impacts.In neighbouring India, Prime Minister Narendra Modi said his government was "prepared to provide Nepal with all possible types of humanitarian assistance". UN Secretary General António Guterres says he is "saddened by the severe flooding", adding that UN teams and partners are mobilising supplies and personnel in Nepal to support the government-led response.The US has promised $500,000 (£367,982) in aid which will be used to cover emergency shelter, water, sanitation and other relief items for communities affected by the floods.Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the UK has offered £5m to help the Nepalese government and will do "everything we can" to support British nationals in Nepal.Figure caption, Aerial footage shows flash flood on Nepal-Tibet borderWhat countries are the missing tourists from?Tourists from all over the world come to Nepal for its mountains and sacred sites. Official figures suggested at least 291 foreigners are among the missing, including: India - the Nepal Tourism board said 288 nationals from neighbouring India were missingChina - The Chinese Foreign Ministry said nearly 100 Chinese nationals are missing in NepalUS - the latest update from Nepal's tourist board is that 65 US tourists are known to be among the missingUkraine - Ukraine's Foreign Ministry said Nepal's Tourist Police informed them 53 Ukrainian nationals were missingMalaysia - 51 Malaysians travelling with Fishtail Tours and Travels are missing in the floods, the board said. An official at the Malaysian embassy in Nepal said more than 50 Malaysians were currently unreachableAustralia - Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has confirmed at least 34 Australian citizens are among the missingUK - Nepal police have confirmed that 33 British nationals are missingCanada - a tourism board spokesman in Nepal said that 24 Canadians have been reported missingSmaller numbers of travellers from South Korea, South Africa, Portugal, the Netherlands and New Zealand are also among the missing.

schema.headline: What we know about deadly Nepal-Tibet floods
